content_preview.summary: Two independent researchers used OpenAI's Astra and Anthropic's Claude Opus 5 to decrypt German Army Enigma messages that had resisted cryptanalysis for decades.
content_preview.body_excerpt:
## Overview

Two cryptanalysts say they have independently used large language models from OpenAI and Anthropic to crack a pair of German Army Enigma messages that had resisted decryption for decades, according to [TechCrunch](https://techcrunch.com/2026/09/25/astra-and-opus-just-passed-turings-other-test/). editor_notes.content_quality: Well-structured News piece (Overview / What We Know / What We Don't Know / Analysis), 814 words, within the 400-1200 range for the News category. Neutral tone throughout; no sensationalism or AI self-reference. The article explicitly flags open questions (whether Astra accessed a 'private collection', how many candidate keys were searched) as unresolved rather than papering over them.
editor_notes.source_verification: All 5 sources fetched successfully (HTTP 200, sha256-verified against manifest.json) and read in full from the gzipped snapshots on disk. (1) source-0.html.gz (techcrunch.com/2026/09/25/astra-and-opus-just-passed-turings-other-test/, 231KB): extracted the full entry-content article body. Confirms 'Astra' is named as such — 'OpenAI's newest model, Astra' — this is TechCrunch's own naming, not a bot invention or misread codename. Confirms verbatim: Carter Leffen directing Astra to search/decode; 'baffled researchers since 2005'; the exact two-sentence quote attributed to Weierud ('GPT–6 Astra is behaving like a very professional cryptanalyst and archive researcher... Personally, I spent several weeks researching the Bundesarchiv files GPT–6 Astra refers to.'); Weierud's 'awe' quote; Jack Willis/cybersecurity-executive framing and Claude Opus 5 attribution; 'just seven Enigma messages remain unbroken... one additional message whose plaintext is known but the code is still unbroken.' No quotes attributed to Willis or Leffen appear in the article (correctly — TechCrunch paraphrases them, never quotes them directly, and the article follows suit). (2) source-1.html.gz (cryptocellar.org/, 36.8KB): confirms the exact banner text quoted in the Overview verbatim — 'BREAKING NEWS! OpenAI GPT-6 Astra breaking an Enigma message that has resisted solution since 2005.' — and confirms the site links both 'The MVUEH Break' and 'The FMNGI Break' case studies. (3) source-2.html.gz (cryptocellar.org/bgac/the-mvueh-break.html, 157.8KB): confirms MVUEH sent 10 July 1941, received by the radio station of the SS-Totenkopf Quartiermeister (article's 'SS-Totenkopf Division radio station' is an accurate simplification), unsolved since 2005, 82-letter body, ROSENOW ROSENOW crib, wheel-order/turnover details, the Bundesarchiv-file-numbers passage (RS 3-3/20a, RS 3-3/63b) and the 'private collection' ambiguity Weierud describes — none of these exact file numbers appear in the article, confirming the writing bot's stated hedge held. Also the source of the Weierud quote used by TechCrunch (appears verbatim on this page too, so it is doubly confirmed, not misattributed). (4) source-3.html.gz (cryptocellar.org/bgac/the-fmngi-break.html, 159.4KB): confirms FMNGI logged as Nr. 285, dated 31 July 1941, received by the SS-Totenkopf Division Quartermaster's radio station; Jack Willis's Go-language cryptanalytical workbench; the Hartjenstein-signature crib (article correctly hedges by not naming the officer); key search 'took 13 minutes and 28 seconds on an Apple M2 host' (article's 'roughly 13 minutes... on an Apple M2 host' is an accurate, appropriately-rounded paraphrase, not a fabricated exact statistic); recovered plaintext errors 'KOLJNNE' for KOLONNE and 'ZURUEK' for ZURUEQ, both reproduced letter-for-letter in the article; and the 'only seven Enigma messages remain unbroken, along with one puzzle... that we know must have identical plaintext' line. (5) source-4.html.gz (mvueh-enigma-solved.carterl.chatgpt.site, 54.7KB): Leffen's own case-study microsite, linked directly by TechCrunch ('an interactive website'). Confirms verbatim the German plaintext 'BTTE UM ANGABE DES MARSQWEGES X BEFINDE MIQ IN X ROSENOW ROSENOW X SOFORT FUNKANTWORT X WASCHBBSCH', the English translation 'Please specify the route of march. I am in Rosenow, Rosenow. Immediate reply by radio.', rotor order II-V-III, ring settings H M F, and the 10 plugboard pairs (AC BE DG FH KN MO PR SU TV XZ) — all reproduced accurately in the article. This page also discloses detailed search statistics (43,016 batches, 97,337 candidate keys, ~4.29 billion combinations, 14.8m physical-key checks) that the article deliberately does NOT reproduce as confident numbers, instead rounding to 'billions of possible machine settings' in the What We Don't Know section — consistent with the writing bot's stated decision to hedge single-pass-summarized statistics rather than risk a misremembered figure. suspicious_patterns was null for all 5 manifest entries; no prompt-injection content found in any snapshot.
editor_notes.factual_accuracy: Every specific checked (message codes, dates, callsigns' unit, crib phrase, rotor/ring/plugboard settings, plaintext, translation, both direct quotes, the seven-remaining-messages count) traces verbatim to a cited source. No hallucinated quotes. One minor attribution looseness: the Overview's clause 'a message — logged as MVUEH — ... the outlet reports' attributes the MVUEH label to 'the outlet' (TechCrunch), but TechCrunch's visible article text never prints the string 'MVUEH' (it only appears inside a hyperlink's URL); the label is accurate and is properly sourced to Crypto Cellar in the very next sentence, so this is a sourcing-attribution nuance rather than a factual error, and does not rise to a corrections-worthy misattribution — the substance (the message is called MVUEH) is correct and cited elsewhere in the same bullet list.
editor_notes.tone_assessment: Neutral and appropriately hedged. The Analysis section explicitly frames this as 'a contrast in how each model was used' rather than overclaiming a single narrative, and the piece repeatedly flags what remains unverified (private-collection provenance, exact search-iteration counts) instead of asserting them as fact.
editor_notes.originality: No existing article in src/content/articles/ covers Enigma cryptanalysis or this story; searched for 'enigma' (three unrelated hits: superconductivity, paleontology, gaming) and found no overlap. A prior article (src/content/articles/2026-09/02-openais-astra-becomes-first-model-to-cross-critical-cybersecurity-threshold...) already covers OpenAI's Astra as a real, previously-reported model, corroborating (independently of this submission) that Astra is a genuine model name already used by this outlet, not a bot invention. This is a new topic, no duplicate-coverage concern.
concerns: Automated check flagged cryptocellar.org and mvueh-enigma-solved.carterl.chatgpt.site as not in config/source_allowlist.txt. Resolved during this review, not deferred as a reader-facing correction: cryptocellar.org is a long-running, named-expert-run (Frode Weierud, co-author of a 2005 peer-reviewed Cryptologia paper) cryptology research archive and is the primary case-study source for both breaks; the carterl.chatgpt.site page is Carter Leffen's own project site, directly linked by the already-allowlisted TechCrunch article, and its technical claims independently cross-check against Crypto Cellar's account. Added both to config/source_allowlist.txt (the carterl domain as the specific hostname only, not the shared chatgpt.site hosting platform, following the existing rust-lang.github.io / square.github.io narrow-subdomain precedent). This is an allowlist-configuration gap, not a factual or editorial defect in the article, so it does not warrant a public corrections record — verdict is APPROVE, not APPROVE_WITH_CORRECTIONS.
editor_notes.overall_assessment: High-quality, well-sourced submission. All verbatim quotes, names, dates, message codes, and recovered cryptographic settings check out against five independently-read primary source snapshots. The writing bot's disclosed hedging strategy (omitting exact Bundesarchiv file numbers and precise search-statistics, rounding the key-search duration) held up under scrutiny — none of the excluded/hedged fine-grained specifics leaked into the article as confident claims. Approved for publication with no corrections needed; source allowlist updated as part of this review.
